HPI: Pt has a history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. He underwent a coronary stent placement in 2018. Diagnostic tests:
1. ECG: ST-segment elevation in leads V1-V4, suggesting an anterior wall STEMI.
2. Troponin levels: Elevated at 2.5 ng/mL (normal range: 0-0.4 ng/mL).
3. CBC, BMP, and coagulation studies were within normal limits.

Diagnosis: Acute anterior wall ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).

Treatment:
1. The patient was immediately taken to the cardiac catheterization lab for an urgent coronary angiography, which revealed a 100% occlusion of the left anterior descending (LAD) artery.
2. Successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with a drug-eluting stent (DES) placement (Boston Scientific SYNERGY™ Everolimus-Eluting Platinum Chromium Coronary Stent System, 3.0 x 20 mm) was performed to restore blood flow to the affected area.
3. The patient was started on dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin and ticagrelor), a beta-blocker (metoprolol), and a high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg) as per the standard of care for STEMI management.

The patient was transferred to the cardiac intensive care unit (CICU) for close monitoring and further management. He remained stable throughout his hospital stay and was discharged on September 10, 2022, with instructions to follow up with his cardiologist, Dr. Michael Chen, within one week and to enroll in a cardiac rehabilitation program.

Discharge medications:
1. Aspirin 81 mg daily
2. Ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily
3. Metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily
4. Atorvastatin 80 mg daily
5. Lisinopril 10 mg daily

Mr. Novak reported sudden onset of sharp, right upper quadrant pain radiating to his back, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. He has a history of gallstones diagnosed 6 months ago, for which he was advised to undergo elective cholecystectomy but has not yet scheduled the procedure.

An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a dilated gallbladder with thickened walls and multiple stones. A stone was visualized in the neck of the gallbladder, suggesting an impacted stone causing acute cholecystitis.

After 24 hours of medical management, the patient's condition improved, and he was scheduled for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy the following day. The surgery was performed successfully without complications, and the patient was discharged 2 days later with prescriptions for oral antibiotics and pain medication.

The patient was instructed to follow up with Dr. Patel at his office at 1365 York Avenue, New York, NY 10021, in one week for wound check and to call the office at (212) 555-1212 in case of any concerns. Mr. O'Connor reported a history of similar episodes in the past, typically occurring after consuming high-fat meals. He also noted associated nausea and vomiting during the current episode. No fever, chills, or changes in bowel habits were reported.

Physical examination revealed:
Vital Signs:
- Blood Pressure: 145/90 mmHg
- Heart Rate: 95 bpm
- Respiratory Rate: 18 breaths/min
- Temperature: 98.8°F (37.1°C)
- SpO2: 97% on room air

Abdominal exam demonstrated tenderness in the right upper quadrant, with positive Murphy's sign. No rebound tenderness, guarding, or rigidity was noted.

Laboratory studies were remarkable for elevated liver function tests and lipase levels:
- AST: 120 U/L (normal range: 5-40 U/L)
- ALT: 150 U/L (normal range: 7-56 U/L)
- Lipase: 250 U/L (normal range: 13-60 U/L)

Subsequent abdominal ultrasound revealed multiple gallstones within the gallbladder, with thickening of the gallbladder wall and pericholecystic fluid. The common bile duct was not dilated.

Based on the clinical presentation, laboratory findings, and imaging studies, the diagnosis of acute calculous cholecystitis was established.

Treatment included:
1. Intravenous fluids (Lactated Ringer's solution)
2. Intravenous antibiotics: Ceftriaxone 1g every 24 hours and Metronidazole 500mg every 8 hours
3. Pain management with intravenous Morphine 4mg every 4 hours as needed
4. NPO (nothing by mouth) status with gradual advancement of diet as tolerated
5. Consultation with the general surgery team for possible cholecystectomy

After 48 hours of conservative management, Mr. O'Connor's symptoms significantly improved, and he was discharged on oral antibiotics (Amoxicillin-Clavulanate 875mg/125mg twice daily) with instructions to follow up with the surgical team within one week for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

Medical Record Number: JHH-1029384756. Patient contact: (410) 515-3000. Email: liam.novak@email.com. Home address: 2468 Maple Street, Baltimore, MD 21218.

The patient reported that the chest pain started suddenly while he was at rest, radiating to his left arm and jaw. The pain was described as pressure-like and was accompanied by diaphoresis and nausea. His past medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a 20-pack-year smoking history.

Upon arrival at the hospital, the patient was immediately assessed by the medical team. His vital signs were: BP 150/90 mmHg, HR 105 bpm, RR 22 breaths/min, SpO2 95% on room air, and Temp 98.8°F. The physical examination revealed diaphoresis, bilateral crackles in the lungs, and an S3 gallop on cardiac auscultation.

The initial ECG showed ST-segment elevations in leads V1-V4, suggesting an acute anterior wall myocardial infarction. The patient was immediately started on oxygen, aspirin, nitroglycerin, and morphine for pain relief. The cardiology team was consulted, and the patient was urgently taken to the catheterization laboratory for a primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI).

In the cath lab, a 95% occlusion of the left anterior descending (LAD) artery was identified. A drug-eluting stent was successfully placed, restoring blood flow to the affected area. The patient was then transferred to the Coronary Care Unit (CCU) for further monitoring and management.

Post-PCI medications included aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, lisinopril, and atorvastatin. The patient remained stable throughout his hospital stay and was discharged on September 10, 2022, with instructions to follow up with his cardiologist, Dr. Michael Chen, within one week. The patient was also referred to a cardiac rehabilitation program and advised to quit smoking.

Discharge diagnoses:
1. Acute anterior wall myocardial infarction
2. Hypertension
3. Hyperlipidemia
4. Tobacco use disorder

The patient was provided with detailed discharge instructions, including medication management, lifestyle modifications, and warning signs of potential complications. A follow-up appointment with Dr. Chen was scheduled for September 17, 2022.

The pain was described as sharp and constant, localized in the right upper quadrant, and radiating to the back. Mr. Novak reported nausea and vomiting twice since the onset of the pain. He also mentioned that his appetite has decreased significantly over the past week.

Mr. Novak's past medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and obesity (BMI 32.5). His current medications are lisinopril 20mg once daily and atorvastatin 40mg once daily. He has no known allergies.

1. Admission to the surgical service
2. NPO status with IV fluid resuscitation
3. IV antibiotics: ceftriaxone 1g every 24 hours and metronidazole 500mg every 8 hours
4. Analgesia with IV morphine as needed
5. Consultation with the general surgery team for possible cholecystectomy

Mr. Novak was educated about his condition, the proposed treatment plan, and potential complications. He consented to the proposed interventions and was admitted for further management.

Emilio Nakamura, a 57-year-old male patient, was brought to the Emergency Department of Stanford Health Care Hospital on June 5, 2023, after experiencing severe chest pain and shortness of breath. Emilio resides at 2465 Campus Drive, Palo Alto, CA 94305. His contact number is (650) 555-2468.

Upon arrival at the hospital, the medical team promptly assessed Emilio's condition. The initial evaluation showed signs of myocardial infarction. Dr. Lisa Chen ordered an urgent ECG and cardiac enzyme tests to confirm the diagnosis.

The ECG revealed ST-segment elevations in leads V1-V4, indicating an anterior wall STEMI. Troponin levels were significantly elevated at 2.6 ng/mL (normal range: <0.04 ng/mL). Dr. Chen immediately initiated treatment protocols for acute myocardial infarction.

Emilio was given aspirin (325 mg), clopidogrel (600 mg), and sublingual nitroglycerin (0.4 mg) for pain relief and to prevent further clot formation in his coronary arteries. Intravenous heparin was also administered for anticoagulation.

The cardiology team led by Dr. Amir Patel performed an emergency percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) within 90 minutes of Emilio's arrival at the hospital through a transradial approach using a drug-eluting stent to restore blood flow in his occluded left anterior descending artery successfully.

Post-procedure care included monitoring vital signs closely as well as cardiac rehabilitation education provided through online resources available on Stanford Health Care's patient portal: https://myhealth.stanfordhealthcare.org/.

Emilio remained stable throughout his hospital stay and was discharged on June 9th with instructions to continue dual antiplatelet therapy consisting of aspirin and clopidogrel daily along with other medications such as beta-blockers and statins prescribed by Dr.Chen for long-term management post-myocardial infarction.

A follow-up appointment has been scheduled with Dr.Patel two weeks post-discharge to assess his progress during recovery following PCI procedure via https://stanfordhealthcare.org/doctorappointment.html or by calling their office directly at his earliest convenience.

5. Educate patient about lifestyle modifications including salt restriction (<2g/day), fluid restriction (<1L/day), regular exercise within limits set by treating physician(s).

- Cardiac rehabilitation program
- Consultation with dietitian

Presenting to Northwestern Memorial Hospital with complaints of severe lower back pain radiating to the left leg for the past week. Patient email: liam.oconnor@email.com. Phone number for contact is (773) 555-2345.

HPI:
Mr. O'Connor reports a history of chronic low back pain managed with NSAIDs and physical therapy. The current episode started after lifting heavy boxes during a recent move. Pain is sharp, constant, and worse with movement or sitting.

PE:
On examination, Mr. O'Connor exhibits tenderness upon palpation of the lumbar paraspinal muscles and decreased range of motion in the lumbar spine due to pain. Straight leg raise test positive at 45 degrees on the left side.

Diagnostic Plan:
Lumbar spine X-rays ordered and completed showing mild degenerative changes without acute fractures or lesions.
MRI lumbar spine recommended to assess for nerve root compression or disc herniation.

Treatment Plan:
1. Prescribed oral steroids (Prednisone) taper dose starting at 40mg daily.
2. Robaxin (Methocarbamol) prescribed for muscle relaxation.
3. Referred to interventional pain management for possible epidural steroid injection if no significant improvement after oral steroid course.
4. Physical therapy sessions twice weekly focusing on core strengthening and flexibility initiated after pain subsides.
5. Follow-up appointment scheduled in two weeks via Telehealth visit through https://mychart.nm.org 

Discharge Instructions provided along with educational resources on low back pain management available at www.spine-health.com/conditions/lower-back-pain/lumbar-degenerative-disc-disease.

Post-procedure care included monitoring in the CCU and initiation of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin and ticagrelor. 3. Cardiovascular Nurse Practitioner Samantha Green for a cardiac rehab assessment on October 3rd

Patient education materials were provided regarding lifestyle modifications post-MI including smoking cessation resources accessible via www.smokefree.gov.

Chief Complaint:
Liam O'Connor, a 58-year-old male, presents with a chief complaint of persistent lower back pain for the past two months. The pain radiates down his left leg and is accompanied by occasional numbness and tingling in his left foot.

History of Present Illness:
The patient reports that the pain started gradually without any specific inciting event. He has tried over-the-counter pain medications such as ibuprofen and acetaminophen with minimal relief. The pain is worse in the morning and improves slightly throughout the day. It is aggravated by prolonged sitting or standing and alleviated by walking or lying down.

- Hypertension, diagnosed 10 years ago, currently managed with lisinopril 20mg daily
- Hyperlipidemia, diagnosed 5 years ago, managed with atorvastatin 20mg daily
- Appendectomy at age 25

Family History:
- Father deceased at age 72 from a myocardial infarction
- Mother alive at age 80 with osteoarthritis and osteoporosis

Social History:
- Non-smoker
- Drinks alcohol occasionally (1-2 drinks per month)
- Retired high school teacher

Physical Examination:
Vital Signs:
- Blood Pressure: 130/85 mmHg
- Heart Rate: 78 bpm
- Respiratory Rate:16 breaths/min 
- Temperature:98.2°F (36.8°C)

Neurological Exam: 
Straight leg raise test positive on left side reproducing radiating leg symptoms; negative on right side.
Strength is normal in all muscle groups of both lower extremities.
Sensory exam shows decreased sensation along lateral aspect left calf extending into dorsum foot.

Assessment/Discussion:
Based on history & physical exam findings most likely diagnosis appears to be Left Sided Lumbar Radiculopathy likely secondary to Lumbar Disc Herniation or Spinal Stenosis affecting L5 &/or S1 nerve roots primarily.

3) Begin Physical Therapy focused on gentle McKenzie exercises for lumbar disc issues starting next week x4 weeks initially.
4) Schedule follow up appointment after completion MRI & initiation PT course in approximately one month's time unless symptoms significantly worsen before then requiring sooner reevaluation here.

Signed,

His primary complaint was severe chest pain radiating to his left arm, which began approximately one hour prior to arrival.

Upon admission, Mr. Novak's vital signs were as follows: Blood Pressure 145/95 mmHg, Heart Rate 105 bpm, Respiratory Rate 22 breaths/min, Temperature 99.1°F (37.3°C), and SpO2 96% on room air. The patient reported a history of hypertension and high cholesterol.

The care team ordered an urgent electrocardiogram (ECG) followed by a complete blood count (CBC), comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), and cardiac enzymes test to evaluate for acute coronary syndrome (ACS). The ECG revealed ST-segment elevations in leads V1-V4 consistent with an anterior wall myocardial infarction.

Interventional cardiologist Dr. Avery Jordan performed an emergent cardiac catheterization using a Philips Allura Xper FD10 cardiovascular X-ray system (Device ID: PXFD10-5544332211). The procedure identified a complete blockage of the left anterior descending artery (LAD), which was treated with two drug-eluting stents.

Post-procedure care included initiation of dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel as well as continuation of beta-blockers for secondary prevention of cardiovascular events. Prior to discharge on September 9th, Mr. Novak received comprehensive education regarding medication adherence and lifestyle modifications via online resources available at www.seattlegrace.org/heart-healthy-living.

Discharge instructions included prescriptions for lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide combination tablet for blood pressure control in addition to statin therapy with atorvastatin calcium tablets for LDL cholesterol reduction per American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association guidelines.

Follow-up appointments were scheduled:
